chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurarah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, al-sadaqah (dower/gift in marriage context) is a later innovation. The people, during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), used to give gifts (nahal) and bestow gifts (hiba), and it was not fitting for one who gave something for the sake of Allah, Exalted and Mighty, to take it back.

He (the Imam) said: 'And as for what was not given for the sake of Allah and in Allah, then he may take it back, whether it was a gift of gratuity (nihlah) or a general gift (hiba), whether it was taken possession of or not.'
And the man shall not take back what he gives to his wife, nor the woman what she gives to her husband, whether it was taken possession of or not.
Is it not that Allah, the Exalted, says: 'And do not take back from them anything you have given them?'
And He said: 'But if they are pleased with you for something of it, then take it in satisfaction and joy.'
And this applies to both the dower (sadaqah) and the gift (hiba).

key_terms.الصَّدَقَةُ: Al-sadaqah; specifically here referring to the dower or a gift given for the sake of God, distinguished from general gifts.
key_terms.حِيزَتْ: Hizat; it was taken possession of (by the recipient).
key_terms.مِمَّا آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ: Mimma ataytumu hunna; from what you have given them (Quranic phrase regarding dower/gifts to wives).
key_terms.نِحْلَةً: Nihlatan; a gift of gratuity or free gift, often implying a specific type of giving.
key_terms.هِبَةً: Hibatan; a general gift, a legal term for gift-giving in Islamic law.
key_terms.يَنْحَلُونَ: Yanhaliuna; they give gifts (from the root n-h-l), referring to the practice of giving gifts of gratuity.
key_terms.يَهَبُونَ: Yahibuna; they bestow gifts (hiba), referring to general gift-giving.

ai.seo_question: Can a husband take back the dower (sadaqah) or gifts given to his wife in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that 'sadaqah' in this context refers to the marital dower given for the sake of God, which is irrevocable, contrasting it with general gifts (hiba) that may be revoked even before possession (huz). The narration explicitly links the Quranic prohibition against reclaiming what is given to wives (4:20) to both dower and general gifts, establishing a legal precedent for the permanence of spousal gifts in Shia jurisprudence. This distinction highlights the theological weight of giving 'for Allah' versus secular gift-giving.
